title: [Experiment, Analysis, and Benchmark] Auditing Batched Semantic COUNT: Fidelity Checks and Full Policy Cost
abstract: Semantic COUNT applies a language-model filter to rows and counts the positive labels. Batching several rows in one request can save calls, but an optimizer may first pay to check whether their labels change. We audit that complete decision by following an existing fidelity check through size selection, full execution and fallback, and measuring the returned result and the cost of every stage. Native LOTUS and a declared custom batch operator are evaluated in 36 configurations over six workloads, two domains and two models, with 16 further policies comparing probe budgets. In the sole accepted batch deployment, all 80 check comparisons agree and full-result disagreement remains below 5%; nevertheless, checking turns the deployment's token saving into a 3.01% increase despite 79.69% fewer requests. Across 12 primary configurations, unchecked random and similarity batches jointly preserve both observed references and reduce requests and raw tokens in one and two cases; the checked policy does so in none. Larger probe budgets retain singleton fallback at higher cost. With caching enabled, all 48 fixed-plan executions use less raw input but more uncached input than their singleton baselines, under the declared repeated-predicate representation. The artifact makes these result targets and complete-cost comparisons reproducible.
keywords: semantic query processing, large language models, COUNT, fidelity certification, prefix caching, query optimization
